prompts.heading: Guiding questions
prompts.lead: Questions and tips from the challenge brief and the project learnings. Use what helps.
prompts.motivation: What motivates customers to connect? Think of cost, comfort, price stability and the end of their old boiler.
prompts.resilience: How can a network here contribute to a resilient, local energy supply and energy security?
prompts.existingBuildings: Existing buildings can usually be connected, most of them even without major thermal renovation.
prompts.heatLineDensity: Heat line density decides the economics: above about 1 MWh per metre of trench, a network can beat individual solutions.
prompts.groundwater: Groundwater is the most economical source, and a micro-network between direct neighbours is a promising start.
prompts.bothDirections: Energy flows both ways in a 5GDHC network, so summer cooling can become a reason to connect.
prompts.extraValue: Look for extra value beyond heat: cooling, stable prices and relief for the electricity grid.
prompts.networkBasics: Water in a 5GDHC network circulates at about 5–25 °C, so renewable energy and waste heat can be used without insulated pipes, and buildings can feed surplus heat back for others. Which local sources and storage could your network connect?
prompts.heatingPlan: The Vienna Heating Plan 2040 sorts areas into district heating, local collective heating (heating neighbourhoods) and individual heating. Does your municipality's heat planning put your area where a collective solution fits?
prompts.whoPays: Who benefits, and who pays? Are they the same people?
prompts.whoOperates: Who owns and who operates the source, the network and the heat pumps?
prompts.distribution: How are investments, revenues and risks shared between the stakeholders?
prompts.ownership: Ownership decides the pathway: utilities, housing associations and private owners each need a different model.
prompts.implementationModels: Think of ownership and operation, organisation and governance, and (re-)financing as one implementation model.
prompts.systemBoundary: Draw the system boundary: who owns the source, the network and the heat pumps?
prompts.costKey: Look for a fair cost key, for example the source by connected load and the pipes by those who use them.
prompts.infrastructure: Think infrastructure: long-term finance, public land and the city as a partner.
prompts.canvasTemplates: Business Model Canvas templates can help you visualise and compare models; use them or your own approach. Focus on economic feasibility, practical implementation and scalability rather than detailed technical design.
prompts.framework: How do energy prices, funding, regulation and long-term commitments affect feasibility?
prompts.reliability: Which risks, dependencies and operational responsibilities must be covered for a reliable and secure supply?
prompts.pipesDriveCost: Pipes and house connections drive the cost; trench length dominates the investment.
prompts.costsFirst: Costs come first: the investment is upfront, the revenues come over 25 to 30 years.
prompts.stayingOut: Every building that stays out raises the cost for the rest.
prompts.voluntary: Connecting is voluntary, and there is no fixed gas phase-out date yet. What makes owners say yes?
prompts.funding: Funding fits only partly and depends on who owns what.
prompts.scaleHere: How can the model be developed and scaled here, and where else could it work?
prompts.whatWorks: What works, what does not, and why? A convincing, critically evaluated model beats a perfect-looking one.
prompts.organisational: Most challenges are organisational rather than technical: coordination, ownership, financing and long-term operation.
prompts.alignment: Align early with the municipality and the authorities: spatial planning, permits and local strategies shape feasibility.
prompts.leadership: Who is the committed initiator? Projects need local leadership and long-term commitment.
prompts.scalableModels: Standardised business and governance models reduce complexity and speed up replication.
prompts.startSmall: Start small: anchor customers, modular growth and micro-networks.
prompts.examplesInPractice: Networks already run in Viertel Zwei, Vienna (decentralised heat pumps on geothermal, wastewater and groundwater), in Bregenz (Lake Constance water, run by the municipal utility) and in Lagarde, Bamberg (about 1,200 dwellings, 70 heat pumps, 5.5 km of pipe). What could your project replicate from them?

how.title: How the AI Plan Score is made
how.body: An AI decision model, Jev by TypeSafe AI, reads the plan step by step, from the first field to the last. It rates each filled part on five evidence levels, from missing to evidenced; empty parts count as 0 without any AI. Gates, yes-or-no questions across the plan, can cap a dimension when something a solid plan must settle is missing. Seven weighted dimensions add up to a score out of 100, shown rounded to 5 with a band of one standard deviation. Below 40 is Early, from 70 on Solid unless a must-have gate failed, and Promising in between. The score is saved in the project and marked outdated once a scored field changes. The Quick Check stays the only calculation.

how.title: How completeness is counted
how.body: Each pitch part has a short list of points. A text point counts when its field has text, a list point when it has an entry, and a risk or critical-assumption point when at least one row is complete and no row is half filled. The share of points covered is the part's score, and the completeness is the average of the six parts. A part is complete when all its points are covered. There is no equation behind this, and no judgement of the content: for an AI opinion on the content, see the AI Plan Score.
